newsitem.title: USA: Modest Feb CPI gain won't alter Fed rate forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Modest Feb CPI gain won't alter Fed rate forecasts.

text.p: Although consumer prices rose a tad more than expected in February, they remained well behaved and should not alter forecasts for or against a Federal Reserve interest rate hike next week, economists said.
The Labor Department said the consumer price index rose 0.3 percent in February, compared to a 0.1 percent rise in January and forecasts for a 0.2 percent increase.
"It does not change the picture very significantly. There is no smoking gun in terms of an outbreak of inflation," said Alison Lynn Reaser, chief economist at Barnett Bank Inc.
"It neither raises nor lowers the probability of a Fed move next week from what the market had been looking for," she added.

The Federal Open Market Committee meets to consider interest rates on March 25. Many Fed officials, including Chairman Alan Greenspan, have said recently that a preemptive interest rate hike might be needed to slow the economy even though there are few solid signs of inflation.
The core rate of retail inflation, which excludes food and energy items, was exactly as expected, showing a benign 0.2 percent rise in February, after a 0.1 percent January rise.

No price change was recorded at the gasoline pump in February and home heating fuel fell 1.9 percent. But overall energy prices rose 0.3 percent in the month as did the cost of consumable goods at the grocery store.
However, a 2.6 percent decline in airline fares did raise a few eyebrows, and forecasters expect this component to cause trouble in upcoming retail price reports.
"One thing to keep in mind is the fact that you did have a decline in airline fares," said Kathleen Stephansen, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp.
"With the excise tax back, certainly that component will start to show some increases. Looking ahead that will be one troublesome part of the report," Stephansen continued.

The February CPI increase, while considered tame, stood in contrast to a huge 0.4 percent drop in producer prices in the month. The slower pace of wholesale price increases could show up in consumer prices in the coming months, economists said.
"The (Bureau of Labor Statistics) admitted under questioning that there are no underlying price pressures," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
"It will take about six months for the surprisingly weak PPI figures to roll through CPI, so it looked like a good report," he added.
The (bond) market, having been pampered recently by the rosy inflation picture, was less than thrilled by the latest price data, economists said.
"We've seen so many good inflation numbers recently, it got jaded to see yet again another good number," Leahey said.
